↩ ◇ Note. The camp arrangement. The camp is described as a square with the Tent of Meeting at its center, three tribes on each of the four sides — east (Judah), south (Reuben), west (Ephraim), north (Dan). The arrangement was read by later mystics as a cosmological diagram: the sanctuary at the center mirrors the divine throne, with Israel arrayed around it like the heavenly host. The Qumran War Scroll reorganizes its eschatological army on exactly this Numbers-2 pattern.

↩ ◇ Note. Levitical service ages. The age range here (30–50) differs from Num 8:24–25 (25–50) and 1 Chr 23:24–27 (20–50). The discrepancies likely reflect different historical periods of cultic practice — earlier and later traditions about how young Levites entered active service. The Mishnah preserves yet another tradition. The Bible’s own multiplicity here is a useful reminder that priestly procedure evolved over centuries.

↩ ◇ Note. The lamp stand. The menorah, made of a single hammered piece of gold (Exod 25:31, 37:17). One of the earliest and most enduring Jewish religious symbols. After the Roman destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE, the menorah taken from the Temple was paraded in Rome — depicted on the Arch of Titus, which still stands in the Forum. The image of that menorah on the Arch is one of the oldest visual representations of any Israelite cultic object that survives.

↩ ◇ Note. A chronological seam. Verse 1 dates events to the first month of year two; chapter 1 verse 1 dates the census to the second month of year two. So Num 9 narratively precedes Num 1. Many readers and the rabbis have noticed this — the book of Numbers is not simply chronological. Possible explanations: thematic organization (cultic preparations 9, then census 1), or composite redaction stitching together earlier material. Either way, the displacement is intentional.

↩ ◇ Note. Re’ach niḥo’aḥ. "Pleasant aroma" — literally "soothing scent." A widely attested ancient Near Eastern image of sacrifice as feeding the gods. The Hebrew Bible inherits the phrase but reshapes its theology — Yahweh does not need food (Ps 50:12–13), and the prophets later mock the idea (Isa 1:11). The phrase persists, however, retained as a poetic technicality even when its underlying mythology is rejected. Compare the demythologized survival of "wings of the wind" (Ps 18:10) and similar inherited imagery.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). FRUIT a word as used in Scripture denoting produce in general, whether vegetable or animal. The Hebrews divided the fruits of the land into three classes:, (1.) The fruit of the field, “corn-fruit” (Hebrews dagan); all kinds of grain and pulse. (2.) The fruit of the vine, “vintage-fruit” (Hebrews tirosh); grapes, whether moist or dried. (3.) “Orchard-fruits” (Hebrews yitshar), as dates, figs, citrons, etc. Injunctions concerning offerings and tithes were expressed by these Hebrew terms alone (Numbers 18:12; Deuteronomy 14:23). This word “fruit” is also used of children or offspring (Genesis 30:2; Deuteronomy 7:13; Luke 1:42; Psalm 21:10; 132:11); also of the progeny of beasts (Deuteronomy 28:51; Isaiah 14:29). It is used metaphorically in a variety of forms (Psalm 104:13; Proverbs 1:31; 11:30; 31:16; Isaiah 3:10; 10:12; Matthew 3:8; 21:41; 26:29; Hebrews 13:15; Romans 7:4, 5; 15:28). The fruits of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22, 23; Ephesians 5:9; James 3:17, 18) are those gracious dispositions and habits which the Spirit produces in those in whom he dwells and works.

↩ ◇ Note. The priestly inheritance. The Levites and priests receive no land — Yahweh himself is their portion. The verse becomes a touchstone for Christian monastic and ministerial traditions (compare Ps 16:5, "Yahweh is my chosen portion"; Ps 73:26). The economic arrangement is significant: by holding no territory, the priestly class was structurally dependent on tithes and offerings, which kept them woven into the lay community rather than sealed off as a landed elite.

↩ ◇ Note. The death of Miriam. Miriam, Aaron, and Moses — the three siblings who led the exodus — die in this same chapter (Miriam 20:1, Aaron 20:28) and the next (Moses, foretold). The triplet death is a structural marker: the wilderness generation passes on. Rabbinic tradition associates Miriam with the well that traveled with Israel (cf. 1 Cor 10:4 in Paul) — when she dies, the water immediately stops (20:2), prompting the rock-striking incident.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Numbers (c. 365 AD)

On the bronze serpent lifted on the standard for the healing of the bitten (Num 21:8-9), Ephrem reads the lifted-up-serpent as the canonical Old-Testament prefigurement of the Crucifixion — taken up verbatim by Christ himself in Jn 3:14: 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up.' The bronze that looks like serpent but contains no venom prefigures Christ-in-the-likeness-of-sinful-flesh-but-without-sin (Rom 8:3). Looking-and-living is the canonical pattern of faith. Tewahedo Mäsqäl theology cites Num 21:8 alongside Jn 3:14 as the canonical doubled-anchor of the Cross-as-healing-standard for the bitten world.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). NEHUSHTAN of copper; a brazen thing a name of contempt given to the serpent Moses had made in the wilderness (Numbers 21:8), and which Hezekiah destroyed because the children of Israel began to regard it as an idol and “burn incense to it.” The lapse of nearly one thousand years had invested the “brazen serpent” with a mysterious sanctity; and in order to deliver the people from their infatuation, and impress them with the idea of its worthlessness, Hezekiah called it, in contempt, “Nehushtan,” a brazen thing, a mere piece of brass (2 Kings 18:4).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SIHON striking down. The whole country on the east of Jordan, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, was possessed by the Amorites, whose king, Sihon, refused to permit the Israelites to pass through his territory, and put his army in array against them. The Israelites went forth against him to battle, and gained a complete victory. The Amorites were defeated; Sihon, his sons, and all his people were smitten with the sword, his walled towns were captured, and the entire country of the Amorites was taken possession of by the Israelites (Numbers 21:21-30; Deuteronomy 2:24-37). The country from the Jabbok to Hermon was at this time ruled by Og, the last of the Rephaim. He also tried to prevent the progress of the Israelites, but was utterly routed, and all his cities and territory fell into the hands of the Israelites (comp. Numbers 21:33-35; Deuteronomy 3:1-14; Psalm 135: 10-12; 136:17-22). These two victories gave the Israelites possession of the country on the east of Jordan, from the Arnon to the foot of Hermon. The kingdom of Sihon embraced about 1,500 square miles, while that of Og was more than 3,000 square miles.

↩ ◇ Note. The taunt-song against Moab. Verses 27–30 are a quoted poetic fragment ("therefore those who speak in proverbs say"). Modern scholarship considers this song one of the earliest preserved Hebrew poems, possibly originating as a Moabite or Amorite victory song that Israel inverted and preserved. Jeremiah 48:45–46 quotes the same lines centuries later — a textual chain that gives a glimpse of how poetic material circulated and was reused across the prophetic tradition.

↩ ◇ Note. The first Balaam oracle. Balaam’s four oracles (chs 23–24) are written in archaic Hebrew, with linguistic features that place them potentially in the early second millennium BCE — among the oldest poetic material in the Pentateuch. The oracles culminate in 24:17 ("a star shall come out of Jacob"), which became the central messianic proof-text of the Bar Kokhba revolt (132–135 CE). Bar Kokhba, "son of the star," was so named precisely from this verse.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. ʼădônây (אֲדֹנָי). the Lord (used as a proper name of God only).

↩ ◇ Note. The Midianite campaign. One of the most ethically difficult chapters in the Pentateuch — total war against Midian, including the killing of male children (31:17), the sparing of female virgins for distribution, and the meticulous division of plunder. Rabbinic and Christian commentary have struggled with this chapter from antiquity. Some readings frame it as judgment on a specific cult-led war (Baal-Peor); others read the text as honest portraiture of how ancient warfare actually was, which the Bible neither endorses nor sanitizes; others read it as ideological theology of the post-exilic compilers projected backward. The chapter resists comfortable resolution.

↩ ◇ Note. The promised borders. Numbers 34 describes the ideal borders of the land — running from the Wadi of Egypt in the south up through Lebo-hamath in the north. These are wider than what Israel ever historically controlled, even at the height of David and Solomon. The chapter has played a role in modern political geography: claims about the "biblical borders of Israel" usually refer back to this passage and to Gen 15:18, neither of which describes the territory of any historical Israelite state.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Numbers (c. 365 AD)

Ephrem reads the threefold Aaronic blessing (Num 6:24-26 — 'The Lord bless thee... make his face shine upon thee... lift up his countenance upon thee') as the canonical priestly anchor that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit may be invoked under three benedictions before the Tabernacle reveals the Trinity. The triadic shape, the divine-face theology, and the placement of the Name upon Israel are read by Ephrem as the seed-form of every later Christian benediction. The Tewahedo Mass (Qǝddase) preserves Num 6:24-26 as the canonical dismissal-blessing; the priest extends the blessing over the people in the exact threefold form, sealing the eucharistic act.

↩ ◇ Note. Birkat Kohanim. The Priestly Blessing — the oldest extant biblical text, attested on the Ketef Hinnom silver amulets (c. 600 BCE). Used in synagogue and church liturgy continuously for nearly three millennia. The three lines progress in meter (3, 5, 7 Hebrew words) and theological scope (preservation, grace, peace). Christian liturgical traditions have preserved it almost untouched in countless ordinaries.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CUCUMBERS (Hebrews plur. kishshuim; i.e., “hard,” “difficult” of digestion, only in Numbers 11:5). This vegetable is extensively cultivated in the East at the present day, as it appears to have been in earlier times among the Hebrews. It belongs to the gourd family of plants. In the East its cooling pulp and juice are most refreshing. “We need not altogether wonder that the Israelites, wearily marching through the arid solitudes of the Sinaitic peninsula, thought more of the cucumbers and watermelons of which they had had no lack in Egypt, rather than of the cruel bondage which was the price of these luxuries.” Groser’s Scripture Natural History. Isaiah speaks of a “lodge” (1:8; Hebrews sukkah), i.e., a shed or edifice more solid than a booth, for the protection throughout the season from spring to autumn of the watchers in a “garden of cucumbers.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GARLIC (Hebrews shum, from its strong odour), mentioned only once (Numbers 11:5). The garlic common in Eastern countries is the Allium sativum or Allium Ascalonicum, so called from its having been brought into Europe from Ascalon by the Crusaders. It is now known by the name of “shallot” or “eschalot.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MELONS only in Numbers 11:5, the translation of the Hebrew abattihim, the LXX. and Vulgate pepones, Arabic britikh. Of this plant there are various kinds, the Egyptian melon, the Cucumus chate, which has been called “the queen of cucumbers;” the water melon, the Cucurbita citrullus; and the common or flesh melon, the Cucumus melo. “A traveller in the East who recollects the intense gratitude which a gift of a slice of melon inspired while journeying over the hot and dry plains, will readily comprehend the regret with which the Hebrews in the Arabian desert looked back upon the melons of Egypt” (Kitto).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ONION The Israelites in the wilderness longed for the “onions and garlick of Egypt” (Numbers 11:5). This was the betsel of the Hebrews, the Allium cepe of botanists, of which it is said that there are some thirty or forty species now growing in Palestine. The onion is “the ‘undivided’ leek, unio, unus, one.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). EYE (Hebrews ‘ain, meaning “flowing”), applied (1) to a fountain, frequently; (2) to colour (Numbers 11:7; R.V., “appearance,” marg. “eye”); (3) the face (Exodus 10:5, 15; Numbers 22:5, 11), in Numbers 14:14, “face to face” (R.V. marg., “eye to eye”). “Between the eyes”, i.e., the forehead (Exodus 13:9, 16). The expression (Proverbs 23:31), “when it giveth his colour in the cup,” is literally, “when it giveth out [or showeth] its eye.” The beads or bubbles of wine are thus spoken of. “To set the eyes” on any one is to view him with favour (Genesis 44:21; Job 24:23; Jeremiah 39:12). This word is used figuratively in the expressions an “evil eye” (Matthew 20:15), a “bountiful eye” (Proverbs 22:9), “haughty eyes” (6:17 marg.), “wanton eyes” (Isaiah 3:16), “eyes full of adultery” (2 Peter 2:14), “the lust of the eyes” (1 John 2:16). Christians are warned against “eye-service” (Ephesians 6:6; Colossians 3:22). Men were sometimes punished by having their eyes put out (1 Samuel 11:2; Samson, Judges 16:21; Zedekiah, 2 Kings 25:7). The custom of painting the eyes is alluded to in 2 Kings 9:30, R.V.; Jeremiah 4:30; Ezekiel 23:40, a custom which still prevails extensively among Eastern women.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Numbers (c. 365 AD)

On the Lord's taking of the Spirit that was upon Moses and putting the same Spirit upon the seventy elders (Num 11:17, 25), Ephrem reads the verse as the canonical Old-Testament antecedent of Pentecost: the one Spirit is shared without diminution, the leader's portion does not decrease when others receive. The seventy elders prefigure both the seventy disciples of Lk 10:1 and the assembled hundred-and-twenty of Acts 1-2. Tewahedo pneumatology cites Num 11:17 + Joel 2:28 as the canonical doubled-Old-Testament-witness to the Pentecost gift of the Spirit on all flesh.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Numbers (c. 365 AD)

On 'Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth' (Num 12:3), Ephrem reads the meekness-of-Moses note as the canonical Old-Testament prefigurement of the Beatitude 'blessed are the meek' (Mt 5:5) and of Christ's own 'I am meek and lowly of heart' (Mt 11:29). Moses' meekness is not weakness but the refusal to defend himself against his own sister and brother; the Lord defends him because he will not. Tewahedo monastic spirituality cites Num 12:3 as the canonical Old-Testament anchor for the cardinal monastic virtue of mätayāqǝbǝr (humility) — the desert father is meek in the pattern of Moses.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Meekness.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. ‘Anav me’od (עָנָו מְאֹד). The narrative aside about Moses’s humility is, ironically, in a book traditionally said to be written by Moses himself — generating a classical interpretive puzzle. The Hebrew ‘anav connotes humility-before-God more than self-deprecation. The very act of bearing this charge from his sister and brother without self-defense (he doesn’t — God does it for him in v.6–8) is the demonstration of the trait.

↩ ‖ Cite. Cross-references. Exo 34:6 · Psa 145:8.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Numbers (c. 365 AD)

On Moses' citation of the divine self-disclosure 'The Lord is longsuffering, and of great mercy, forgiving iniquity and transgression... by no means clearing the guilty' (Num 14:18), Ephrem reads the formula as the canonical liturgical prayer-of-pardon adopted into the Septuagint Psalter (Ps 86:15, 103:8, 145:8) and extended into every later Christian confession-rite. The verse holds together the two halves of the Name: mercy and justice, neither cancelling the other. Tewahedo penance liturgy (näsḫa-of-näsḫa) cites Num 14:18 as the canonical Old-Testament anchor for the priestly absolution formula; the same formula governs the Lenten qǝne and the Holy Thursday foot-washing.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Goat, The, Long-Suffering of God, The, Mercy of God, The.

↩ ◇ Note. Citing the Thirteen Attributes. Moses’s intercession in Numbers 14 cites Exodus 34:6–7 — the first inner-biblical citation of the divine self-description. Throughout the prophetic books and psalms, the Thirteen Attributes formula appears whenever Israel needs to plead for mercy. The intertextual pattern is itself the theology: God is who he said he was at Sinai.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ABIRAM father of height; i.e., “proud.” (1.) One of the sons of Eliab, who joined Korah in the conspiracy against Moses and Aaron. He and all the conspirators, with their families and possessions (except the children of Korah), were swallowed up by an earthquake (Numbers 16:1-27; 26:9; Psalm 106:17). (2.) The eldest son of Hiel the Bethelite, who perished prematurely in consequence of his father’s undertaking to rebuild Jericho (1 Kings 16:34), according to the words of Joshua (6:26). (See JERICHO.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DATHAN welled; belonging to a fountain, a son of Eliab, a Reubenite, who joined Korah (q.v.) in his conspiracy, and with his accomplices was swallowed up by an earthquake (Numbers 16:1; 26:9; Deuteronomy 11:6; Psalm 106:17).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ELIAB to whom God is father. (1.) A Reubenite, son of Pallu (Numbers 16:1, 12; 26:8, 9; Deuteronomy 11:6). (2.) A son of Helon, and chief of the tribe of Zebulun at the time of the census in the wilderness (Numbers 1:9; 2:7). (3.) The son of Jesse, and brother of David (1 Samuel 16:6). It was he who spoke contemptuously to David when he proposed to fight Goliath (1 Samuel 17:28). (4.) One of the Gadite heroes who joined David in his stronghold in the wilderness (1 Chronicles 12:9).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PELETH swiftness. (1.) A Reubenite whose son was one of the conspirators against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16:1). (2.) One of the sons of Jonathan (1 Chronicles 2:33).

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Numbers (c. 365 AD)

On the swallowing of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram by the earth (Num 16:32), Ephrem reads the judgment-against-priestly-rebellion as the canonical anchor of the gravity-of-priesthood: those who usurp the priestly office without divine appointment fall through the very earth that should bear them. Korah's rebellion is doubled in Jude 11 ('perished in the gainsaying of Core') and read as type of every later schismatic seizure of office. Tewahedo canon-law cites Num 16:32 + Jude 11 as the canonical doubled-warrant for the gravity of unauthorised priesthood; only the lawfully-ordained may approach the tabot.

↩ ◇ Note. Korah’s legacy. The censers of the rebels are hammered into a covering for the altar — a permanent reminder that only Aaron’s line may offer incense. But the descendants of Korah live on in scripture: the "sons of Korah" are credited with eleven psalms (Pss 42, 44–49, 84–85, 87–88), some of the most beautiful in the psalter. The text resists treating the rebels’ family as a permanently cursed line.

↩ ◇ Note. Nehushtan / John 3:14. The bronze serpent on a pole, lifted up, healing those who look on it — Jesus invokes this in John 3:14–15 ("as Moses lifted up the serpent… so must the Son of Man be lifted up"). The cross becomes the new nehushtan. Later this same bronze object becomes an idol that Hezekiah destroys (2 Kings 18:4) — a sign that even legitimate signs of grace can become objects of false worship.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. ʼădônây (אֲדֹנָי). the Lord (used as a proper name of God only).

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Numbers (c. 365 AD)

On the Lord's opening of the mouth of Balaam's ass to rebuke the prophet (Num 22:28), Ephrem reads the wonder as the canonical anchor of the doctrine that the Lord may speak truth from the most unworthy vessels: a Gentile diviner is humbled by his own beast, and the prophecy that follows (Num 24:17) issues from the same mouth that needed an ass's instruction. The verse becomes the typological seed of 2 Peter 2:16's denunciation of Balaam — and of the broader patristic principle that the prophetic gift can pass through mouths whose private life condemns them. Tewahedo pastoral theology cites Num 22:28 as the canonical Old-Testament anchor: receive the word for its truth, not for the messenger's worthiness.

The Deir Alla Inscription (8th–7th c. BCE), found in Jordan, mentions "Balaam son of Beor, the seer of the gods" — confirming Balaam’s historical reputation as a famous diviner of the region, independent of the biblical text.

↩ ◇ Note. Divine constancy and divine relenting. The verse declares God does not nicham (relent, change his mind). Yet other texts (Gen 6:6, Exod 32:14, 1 Sam 15:11) say he does. Two classical resolutions: (1) God’s essential will is unchanging; his expressed dispositions respond to human action; (2) anthropomorphic language is being qualified. Moses Maimonides reads this as a teaching about the limits of all human language about God.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ALOES (Hebrews ‘ahalim), a fragrant wood (Numbers 24:6; Psalm 45:8; Proverbs 7:17; Cant. 4:14), the Aquilaria agallochum of botanists, or, as some suppose, the costly gum or perfume extracted from the wood. It is found in China, Siam, and Northern India, and grows to the height sometimes of 120 feet. This species is of great rarity even in India. There is another and more common species, called by Indians aghil, whence Europeans have given it the name of Lignum aquile, or eagle-wood. Aloewood was used by the Egyptians for embalming dead bodies. Nicodemus brought it (pounded aloe-wood) to embalm the body of Christ (John 19:39); but whether this was the same as that mentioned elsewhere is uncertain. The bitter aloes of the apothecary is the dried juice of the leaves Aloe vulgaris.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). LIGN-ALOES (only in pl., Hebrews ‘ahalim), a perfume derived from some Oriental tree (Numbers 24:6), probably the agallochum or aloe-wood. (See ALOES).

He lived at the time of the Exodus. (2.) Another king of the Amalekites whom Saul spared unlawfully, but whom Samuel on his arrival in the camp of Saul ordered, in retributive justice (Judges 1), to be brought out and cut in pieces (1 Samuel 15:8-33. Comp. Exodus 17:11; Numbers 14:45).

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Numbers (c. 365 AD)

On Balaam's fourth oracle — 'I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel' (Num 24:17) — Ephrem reads the doubled-image (Star + Sceptre) as the canonical Old-Testament prophecy of the Messiah's advent: the Star is the sign that appears to the Gentile Magi (Mt 2:2 — 'we have seen his star in the east'), the Sceptre is the Davidic kingship received by the Son of David. The Gentile diviner Balaam prophesies through gritted teeth the salvation of the world. Tewahedo nativity-iconography cites Num 24:17 as the canonical Old-Testament doubled-anchor of the Star-of-Bethlehem and the Davidic-Solomonic Sceptre — both inherited by the Tewahedo Solomonic dynasty's self-understanding.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SHETH tumult. (1.) “The children of Sheth” (Numbers 24:17); R.V., “the sons of tumult,” which is probably the correct rendering, as there is no evidence that this is a proper name here. (2.) The antediluvian patriarch (1 Chronicles 1:1).

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Christ, the King, Moabites, Stars, The, Titles and Names of Christ.

↩ ◇ Note. Balaam’s messianic oracle. Read messianically in Second Temple Judaism (Dead Sea Scroll 4QTestimonia, 1QM), in early Christianity (the Magi in Matthew 2 recognize the star), and in later Jewish tradition (Bar Kokhba’s name = "son of the star," claimed in the 132 CE revolt). The verse stands at one of the highest concentrations of inter-religious messianic interpretation.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: DAUGHTER, GILEAD, HEPHER, HOGLAH, MANASSEH, NAPHTALI, REUBEN, SIMEON, ZEBULUN.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MAHLAH disease, one of the five daughters of Zelophehad (Numbers 27:1-11) who had their father’s inheritance, the law of inheritance having been altered in their favour.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ZELOPHEHAD first-born, of the tribe of Manasseh, and of the family of Gilead; died in the wilderness. Having left no sons, his daughters, concerned lest their father’s name should be “done away from among his family,” made an appeal to Moses, who, by divine direction, appointed it as “a statute of judgment” in Israel that daughters should inherit their father’s portion when no sons were left (Numbers 27:1-11). But that the possession of Zelophehad might not pass away in the year of jubilee from the tribe to which he belonged, it was ordained by Moses that his daughters should not marry any one out of their father’s tribe; and this afterwards became a general law (Numbers 36).

↩ ◇ Note. The Zelophehad case. Five sisters, no brother — they petition for inheritance and win. The case becomes the legal precedent for female inheritance in Israel (with the qualifying ruling at Num 36 that they must marry within their tribe to keep land in family). The narrative is unusually procedural: human petition, divine answer, legal codification — a microcosm of how case law develops in the Pentateuch.

↩ ◇ Note. The princes’ wagons. The chapter — at 89 verses, the longest in Numbers — opens with the tribal princes’ collective gift of six covered wagons and twelve oxen for transporting the Tabernacle. Moses distributes them according to need: two wagons to the Gershonites (lighter loads — curtains, hangings), four to the Merarites (heavier loads — frames, bars, pillars), none to the Kohathites because they carry the most sacred objects on their shoulders (7:9, the rationale repeated from 4:15 — these objects must not even be touched by transport vehicles). The distribution illustrates a recurring Pentateuchal principle: holiness gradients translate directly into logistical procedure. The chapter’s subsequent monotonous repetition — the same offering listed twelve times, once per tribe (7:12–83) — has frustrated readers but registers theologically: the princes are equal in honor before Yahweh, and the text refuses to abbreviate that equality even at the cost of readability.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CHARGER a bowl or deep dish. The silver vessels given by the heads of the tribes for the services of the tabernacle are so named (Numbers 7:13, etc.). The “charger” in which the Baptist’s head was presented was a platter or flat wooden trencher (Matthew 14:8, 11; Mark 6:25, 28). The chargers of gold and silver of Ezra 1:9 were probably basins for receiving the blood of sacrifices.

↩ ◇ Note. The voice from the mercy seat. The chapter closes with one of the OT’s most theologically charged sentences: Moses enters the Tent of Meeting and hears the divine voice "from above the mercy seat (kapporet) that was on the ark of the Testimony, from between the two cherubim." The geometry is precise — the voice emerges from the empty space framed by the cherubim’s wings, atop the ark. The same configuration appears at Exod 25:22 and lies behind the Davidic title for Yahweh "enthroned between the cherubim" (1 Sam 4:4, 2 Sam 6:2, Pss 80:1, 99:1). The arrangement encodes Israel’s aniconic theology with surgical precision: the empty space between the guardian-figures is the divine throne — not a statue, not an image, but the framed absence in which the deity speaks. The Letter to the Hebrews (Heb 9:5) takes the verse as foundational for its argument about the inner sanctuary that Christ enters.

↩ ◇ Note. The budded rod. Following the Korah rebellion (ch 16), Yahweh resolves priestly disputation by miraculous sign: twelve rods, one per tribe, are placed before the Ark; only Aaron’s buds, blossoms, and bears almonds overnight. The almond-tree symbolism is theologically dense: the Hebrew name shaqed ("almond") puns on shoqed ("watching, hastening"), and the same imagery returns in Jer 1:11–12, where the almond-rod sign signals Yahweh’s active oversight of his word. Aaron’s rod becomes one of three sacred objects placed inside the Ark (Heb 9:4: the rod, the manna jar, the tablets), though the placement is debated — 1 Kgs 8:9 says only the tablets remained in the Ark by Solomon’s temple. The chapter is the OT’s definitive establishment of the Aaronide priestly monopoly through visible miracle, settling a question that the Korah rebellion had attempted to reopen.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: MIRACLES, TABERNACLE.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Numbers (c. 365 AD)

On Aaron's rod that 'budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds' (Num 17:8), Ephrem reads the blossoming-of-the-dead-staff as the canonical Marian-rod typology: a dry rod brings forth life out of season because the Lord wills it, prefiguring the Virgin who bears the Word without seed. The Tewahedo Wǝddase Maryam preserves this reading explicitly — Mary is the 'rod of Aaron' (in Geʿez: bä-ṭwāf zä-Aron) whose blossoming is the seedless Conception of the Word. Num 17:8 is therefore the canonical Old-Testament Marian-iconographic anchor in Ethiopian devotion, alongside the burning bush (Ex 3:2) and the ladder of Jacob (Gen 28:12 + Jub 27:19).

↩ ◇ Note. The rod kept as warning. The budded rod is preserved before the Ark not as relic alone but as cautionary monument — a permanent visual deterrent against future challenges to Aaronide priestly prerogative. The Hebrew l’ot l’v’nei meri ("for a sign for the sons of rebellion") echoes the language used of the bronze censers of Korah’s company, which were beaten into a covering for the altar (Num 16:38–40). The pattern — defeated rebellions converted into permanent cult-objects warning against repetition — is one of Israel’s recurring institutional moves: failure becomes liturgy. The Christian transposition appears at 1 Cor 10:11 ("these things happened to them as examples and were written for our instruction"); the OT is to be read as standing warning rather than as completed history. The chapter’s placement immediately before the priestly-Levitical legislation of ch 18 makes the institutional point: the warning establishes the framework within which the duties of the priesthood are then specified.

↩ ◇ Note. The second census and the inheritance principle. The chapter conducts the second wilderness census (the first was Num 1, before the rebellion); 26:64–65 records the staggering attrition — of all those originally numbered, only Joshua and Caleb remain alive. The new census is not just a population audit but the basis for land-allotment: tribal portions in Canaan will be sized in proportion to current numbers (26:54), with the actual locations determined by lot (26:55–56). The principle combines proportional fairness (size of tribe → size of inheritance) with submission to divine designation (lot → location), and it shapes the Joshua allotment chapters directly. The chapter is the institutional foundation for Israel’s entire theology of land tenure — inheritances are not simply seized but received as divinely apportioned tribal patrimony, a conception that underwrites the later Jubilee land-return laws (Lev 25) and the prophetic critiques of land-accumulation (Isa 5:8, Mic 2:1–2).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MERARITES the descendants of Merari (Numbers 26:57). They with the Gershonites and the Kohathites had charge of the tabernacle, which they had to carry from place to place (Numbers 3:20, 33-37; 4:29-33). In the distribution of the oxen and waggons offered by the princes (Numbers 7), Moses gave twice as many to the Merarites (four waggons and eight oxen) as he gave to the Gershonites, because the latter had to carry only the lighter furniture of the tabernacle, such as the curtains, hangings, etc., while the former had to carry the heavier portion, as the boards, bars, sockets, pillars, etc., and consequently needed a greater supply of oxen and waggons. This is a coincidence illustrative of the truth of the narrative. Their place in marching and in the camp was on the north of the tabernacle. The Merarites afterwards took part with the other Levitical families in the various functions of their office (1 Chronicles 23:6, 21-23; 2 Chronicles 29:12, 13). Twelve cities with their suburbs were assigned to them (Joshua 21:7, 34-40).

↩ ◇ Note. The Mosaic genealogy. The verse names Moses’ mother Jochebed as Levi’s own daughter, born "to Levi in Egypt" — a chronology that, on its face, requires Jochebed to be at least 250 years old when Moses is born, since the Egyptian sojourn is portrayed as 430 years (Exod 12:40). The same difficulty appears at Exod 6:20 and Num 26:59. Most modern critical readers (so de Vaux, Sarna) treat the Mosaic genealogy as preserving a schematic rather than a literal lineage — Jochebed is "of the daughters of Levi" in the sense of belonging to that tribe, not a literal daughter of the patriarch. The schematic reading also explains the otherwise impossible compression of generations between Joseph and Moses (only four: Levi → Kohath → Amram → Moses) within the long Egyptian sojourn. The verse is one of the OT’s clearest cases of genealogical telescoping, where representative ancestors stand for entire generations, common in ANE and biblical genealogical practice.

↩ ◇ Note. Sh’mini Atzeret — the eighth day. An additional one-day festival appended to the seven days of Sukkot — Yahweh’s additional request that Israel "linger" (the Hebrew atzeret connotes "stopping, not going home yet") for one more day of holy assembly. The day is treated as a separate festival in Jewish liturgical practice (cf. Lev 23:36), with its own offerings (one bull, not the descending series of Sukkot proper). The rabbinic reading (Rashi at Lev 23:36) imagines Yahweh as a king reluctant to part from his guests after the great Sukkot pilgrimage: "your departure is hard for me — stay one more day." The eighth day’s symbolic afterlife is significant: in Christian thought it becomes the day of the resurrection (the day after the Sabbath, hence "the eighth day" of patristic reflection — Justin, Augustine), with the eight-sided baptismal fonts of late-antique churches deliberately echoing the symbolism. The Numbers framework is the OT root of the "eighth day" theology that runs through later Christian liturgical reflection.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. ʼădônây (אֲדֹנָי). the Lord (used as a proper name of God only).

↩ ◇ Note. The vow law. The chapter codifies one of Israel’s most binding speech-acts: a vow uttered to Yahweh creates an obligation the speaker cannot retract on his own. The principle has wide-ranging consequences in the rest of the OT — Jephthah’s rash vow (Judg 11:30–40) and Saul’s adjuration (1 Sam 14:24, 39) both stage tragic failures to navigate the principle. Eccl 5:4–5 ("when you vow a vow, do not delay paying it… better not to vow than to vow and not pay") turns the principle into wisdom literature; Jesus’ "do not swear at all" (Matt 5:34) extends the same anxiety toward all speech-acts. The verse is the institutional foundation for Israelite vow-piety, including the Nazirite tradition (Num 6) and the lifelong dedications of Hannah’s child (1 Sam 1:11) and various other named figures. The chapter takes the binding power of speech with deadly seriousness — and immediately, in the verses that follow, complicates it through the case-law of female vows.

↩ ◇ Note. The husband’s veto. The chapter’s case-law on female vows establishes that a husband (or, for unmarried women, a father) has authority to nullify his wife’s or daughter’s vows on the day he hears them — but if he says nothing that day, the vow stands binding. The provision combines patriarchal hierarchy with significant constraint: the male veto is not perpetual but day-of-hearing only, and silence becomes consent. Modern feminist readings have grappled with the chapter from multiple angles — Ilana Pardes and Tikva Frymer-Kensky read the case-law as preserving real female religious agency within a framework that limits its scope; older readings emphasize the constraint exclusively. The chapter is unusual in OT law for explicitly addressing female-initiated cultic action and providing detailed procedural rules for it — an acknowledgment that women regularly made vows and the legal system needed to address them, even if the procedural answer reflects the hierarchies of the surrounding culture. The verse remains one of the most-discussed in feminist OT scholarship.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). JAAZER he (God) helps, a city of the Amorites on the east of Jordan, and assigned, with neighbouring places in Gilead, to Gad (Numbers 32:1, 35; Joshua 13:25). It was allotted to the Merarite Levites (21:39). In David’s time it was occupied by the Hebronites, i.e., the descendants of Kohath (1 Chronicles 26:31). It is mentioned in the “burdens” proclaimed over Moab (Isaiah 16:8, 9; Jeremiah 48:32). Its site is marked by the modern ruin called Sar or Seir, about 10 miles west of Amman, and 12 from Heshbon. “The vineyards that once covered the hill-sides are gone; and the wild Bedawin from the eastern desert make cultivation of any kind impossible.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ATAROTH crowns. (1.) A city east of Jordan, not far from Gilead (Numbers 32:3). (2.) A town on the border of Ephraim and Benjamin (Joshua 16:2, 7), called also Ataroth-adar (16:5). Now ed-Da’rieh. (3.) “Ataroth, the house of Joab” (1 Chronicles 2:54), a town of Judah inhabited by the descendants of Caleb.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ELEALEH God has ascended, a place in the pastoral country east of Jordan, in the tribe of Reuben (Numbers 32:3, 37). It is not again mentioned till the time of Isaiah (15:4; 16:9) and Jeremiah (48:34). It is now an extensive ruin called el-A’al, about one mile north-east of Heshbon.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). NIMRAH pure, a city on the east of Jordan (Numbers 32:3); probably the same as Beth-nimrah (Joshua 13:27). It has been identified with the Nahr Nimrin, at one of the fords of Jordan, not far from Jericho.

↩ ◇ Note. The Reubenite-Gadite request. Reuben and Gad ask to settle in Trans-Jordan rather than crossing the Jordan with the rest of Israel — the rich grasslands east of the river suit their abundant herds. Moses’ initial reaction (vv. 6–15) treats the request as a recurrence of the Kadesh-barnea rebellion (cf. ch 13–14), where the spies’ report led to forty years of wandering. The negotiated resolution (vv. 16–32) requires the trans-Jordanian tribes to send their fighting men across with the rest of Israel until the conquest is completed. The arrangement creates the structural feature of Israel-in-Trans-Jordan that runs through the OT — Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh permanently occupy territory east of the Jordan, with periodic political and religious tensions about whether they truly belong to "Israel proper" (cf. Josh 22, the altar dispute; 1 Chr 5:25–26, their early Assyrian deportation). The chapter is the foundation of the Trans-Jordanian Israelite identity that complicates Israelite geography for the rest of the canon.

↩ ◇ Note. The double accountability formula. Moses’ resolution requires the Trans-Jordanian tribes to be clear before both Yahweh and Israel — the obligation runs in two directions, vertical and horizontal, and discharge requires both. The dual-accountability formula recurs throughout OT covenant theology: covenants between Yahweh and Israel always also imply obligations among Israelites themselves, because Yahweh’s honor and Israel’s communal welfare cannot be separated. The same principle drives Lev 19:18 ("love your neighbor as yourself"), framed as covenant fidelity rather than as ethics; the prophetic critiques (Amos, Mic) treat exploitation of fellow Israelites as automatically a religious offense against Yahweh. The verse encodes the principle compactly: there is no faithful covenant relationship with the deity that does not also discharge obligation to the human community. The two-fold accountability becomes one of the structural features of OT moral-religious theology.

↩ ◇ Note. The wilderness itinerary. The chapter preserves a 42-stage itinerary of Israel’s wilderness wandering, from Rameses to the plains of Moab. The list is one of the OT’s most concentrated geographic-historical documents — in compressed form it traces the entire forty-year period through named encampments, many otherwise unattested. The list’s topographical realism has supported decades of attempted route-reconstruction (the "exodus route" debates), though the identification of specific sites remains contested for most of the catalog. Beyond geography, the list functions theologically: each named site is, for the original audience, a memory-trigger for an episode the audience knows from the surrounding narrative (Marah, Sinai, Kadesh, Hor). The chapter compresses the entire Pentateuchal wilderness experience into a memorial list — the same compression that Pss 78, 105, 106, and 136 perform with the same material in poetic form. The genre is itinerary-as-confession, an Israelite literary form recurrent across the canon.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). LIBNAH transparency; whiteness. (1.) One of the stations of the Israelites in the wilderness (Numbers 33:20, 21). (2.) One of the royal cities of the Canaanites taken by Joshua (Joshua 10:29-32; 12:15). It became one of the Levitical towns in the tribe of Judah (21:13), and was strongly fortified. Sennacherib laid siege to it (2 Kings 19:8; Isaiah 37:8). It was the native place of Hamutal, the queen of Josiah (2 Kings 23:31). ↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). EZION-GEBER the giant’s backbone (so called from the head of a mountain which runs out into the sea), an ancient city and harbour at the north-east end of the Elanitic branch of the Red Sea, the Gulf of Akabah, near Elath or Eloth (Numbers 33:35; Deuteronomy 2:8). Here Solomon built ships, “Tarshish ships,” like those trading from Tyre to Tarshish and the west, which traded with Ophir (1 Kings 9:26; 2 Chronicles 8:17); and here also Jehoshaphat’s fleet was shipwrecked (1 Kings 22:48; 2 Chronicles 20:36). It became a populous town, many of the Jews settling in it (2 Kings 16:6, “Elath”). It is supposed that anciently the north end of the gulf flowed further into the country than now, as far as ‘Ain el-Ghudyan, which is 10 miles up the dry bed of the Arabah, and that Ezion-geber may have been there.

↩ ◇ Note. The conquest mandate. Moses’ command that Israel destroy all Canaanite idols, molten images, and high places on entering the land is one of the OT’s most stringent anti-syncretism texts. The vocabulary is precise — maskiyyotam (engraved or figured stones), tzalmei masseikhotam (molten images), bamot (high places) — names every category of cult-object the surrounding peoples used. The instruction is repeated and intensified in Deut 7:5, 12:2–3 and represents one of the strongest streams of Pentateuchal anti-syncretist theology. The historical question of how thoroughly this was ever carried out is sharply contested: Judg 1–2 admits widespread incompleteness, the books of Kings repeatedly record that high places remained, and archaeological evidence (Iron Age I–II Israelite household and rural cult sites) suggests substantial syncretism throughout the monarchic period. The chapter encodes the program; the rest of the OT records its uneven application.

↩ ◇ Note. The cities of refuge. The chapter institutes one of OT law’s most remarkable provisions — six designated cities (three on each side of the Jordan, Num 35:14) where a person who has killed someone unintentionally may flee from the blood-avenger (the go’el ha-dam) of the deceased. The institution preserves blood-vengeance as a recognized legal mechanism while creating a legal sanctuary that distinguishes intentional from unintentional killing — the OT’s clearest articulation of the criminal-law distinction we now call mens rea. The cities are listed in Josh 20:7–8 (Kedesh, Shechem, Hebron, Bezer, Ramoth-gilead, Golan), all of them Levitical cities, integrating cultic and judicial functions in the same spaces. Heb 6:18 takes the cities of refuge as theological figure for Christian salvation ("we who have fled for refuge"). The institution is one of the OT’s most institutionally creative innovations and has had long influence on the development of asylum law in Western legal systems.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MURDER Wilful murder was distinguished from accidental homicide, and was invariably visited with capital punishment (Numbers 35:16, 18, 21, 31; Leviticus 24:17). This law in its principle is founded on the fact of man’s having been made in the likeness of God (Genesis 9:5, 6; John 8:44; 1 John 3:12, 15). The Mosiac law prohibited any compensation for murder or the reprieve of the murderer (Exodus 21:12, 14; Deuteronomy 19:11, 13; 2 Samuel 17:25; 20:10). Two witnesses were required in any capital case (Numbers 35:19-30; Deuteronomy 17:6-12). If the murderer could not be discovered, the city nearest the scene of the murder was required to make expiation for the crime committed (Deuteronomy 21:1-9). These offences also were to be punished with death, (1) striking a parent; (2) cursing a parent; (3) kidnapping (Exodus 21:15-17; Deuteronomy 27:16).

↩ ◇ Note. The amnesty of the high priest’s death. The killer who has fled to a city of refuge must remain there until the death of the current high priest, at which point he may return home and the blood-avenger may no longer pursue him. The provision is one of the OT’s strangest legal mechanisms: the high priest’s death functions as a kind of amnesty event that wipes the slate of unintentional bloodguilt for everyone currently in refuge. The theological logic, as developed by the rabbinic tradition (b. Makkot 11b) and Christian commentators (Heb 9:11–28 makes extensive Christological use of the parallel), treats the high priest’s death as cultically representative — his death "covers" the bloodguilt of those under refuge. The Letter to the Hebrews develops the analogy explicitly: Christ’s death functions as the eschatological high-priestly death that releases all who have fled for refuge to him. The verse is one of the OT’s richer examples of how a peculiar legal procedure becomes theological resource for later interpretive traditions.

↩ ◇ Note. Sukkot offerings — and the seventy bulls. The Feast of Tabernacles requires an extraordinary descending series of bull offerings: thirteen on day one, twelve on day two, eleven on day three, and so on, totaling seventy bulls across the seven main festival days (29:13–32). Rabbinic interpretation (b. Sukkah 55b) reads the seventy bulls as offerings on behalf of the seventy nations of the world — Israel sacrificing for universal benefit at the festival that anticipates the eschatological gathering of nations to Zion (cf. Zech 14:16, where Sukkot is the festival the surviving nations will keep at Jerusalem in the messianic age). The descending count itself has been variously interpreted; some readers see numerological diminishment as the festival winds down, others read it as a deliberate inversion of mounting violence (more sacrifices on day one when the most peace-offering is needed). Sukkot’s peculiar offerings make it the most universalistic of the Israelite festivals.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ENSIGN (1.) Hebrews ‘oth, a military standard, especially of a single tribe (Numbers 2:2). Each separate tribe had its own “sign” or “ensign.” (2.) Hebrews nes, a lofty signal, as a column or high pole (Numbers 21:8, 9); a standard or signal or flag placed on high mountains to point out to the people a place of rendezvous on the irruption of an enemy (Isaiah 5:26; 11:12; 18:3; 62:10; Jeremiah 4:6, 21; Psalm 60:4). This was an occasional signal, and not a military standard. Elevation and conspicuity are implied in the word. (3.) The Hebrew word degel denotes the standard given to each of the four divisions of the host of the Israelites at the Exodus (Numbers 1:52; 2:2; 10:14). In Cant. 2:4 it is rendered “banner.” We have no definite information as to the nature of these military standards. (See BANNER.)

↩ ◇ Note. The encampment geometry. The chapter describes Israel’s wilderness encampment as a precise quadrilateral: three tribes on each side (east, south, west, north) of a central core occupied by the Levites and the Tent of Meeting. The arrangement is theologically deliberate — the divine sanctuary at the geometric center, surrounded by the priestly tribe, surrounded in turn by the laity — and it formalizes a principle that runs through the rest of the OT: holiness is concentric, with degrees of access calibrated by proximity to the central sanctuary (cf. the temple’s nested courts in Ezek 40–48, the ANE temple-mountain ideology). The 12-tribes-around-a-central-axis pattern also has astrological-cosmological resonances in some rabbinic readings (the twelve tribes as the twelve zodiacal signs, the tabernacle as cosmic axis), though the OT itself does not develop these connections explicitly. The verse encodes Israel’s self-conception as a sanctified community organized around divine presence rather than around a king or military leader.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BIRTHRIGHT (1.) This word denotes the special privileges and advantages belonging to the first-born son among the Jews. He became the priest of the family. Thus Reuben was the first-born of the patriarchs, and so the priesthood of the tribes belonged to him. That honour was, however, transferred by God from Reuben to Levi (Numbers 3:12, 13; 8:18). (2.) The first-born son had allotted to him also a double portion of the paternal inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:15-17). Reuben was, because of his undutiful conduct, deprived of his birth-right (Genesis 49:4; 1 Chronicles 5:1). Esau transferred his birth-right to Jacob (Genesis 25:33). (3.) The first-born inherited the judicial authority of his father, whatever it might be (2 Chronicles 21:3). By divine appointment, however, David excluded Adonijah in favour of Solomon. (4.) The Jews attached a sacred importance to the rank of “first-born” and “first-begotten” as applied to the Messiah (Romans 8:29; Colossians 1:18; Hebrews 1:4-6). As first-born he has an inheritance superior to his brethren, and is the alone true priest.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SHIMEI famous. (1.) A son of Gershon, and grandson of Levi (Numbers 3:18; 1 Chronicles 6:17, 29); called Shimi in Exodus 6:17. (2.) A Benjamite of the house of Saul, who stoned and cursed David when he reached Bahurim in his flight from Jerusalem on the occasion of the rebellion of Absalom (2 Samuel 16:5-13). After the defeat of Absalom he “came cringing to the king, humbly suing for pardon, bringing with him a thousand of his Benjamite tribesmen, and representing that he was heartily sorry for his crime, and had hurried the first of all the house of Israel to offer homage to the king” (19:16-23). David forgave him; but on his death-bed he gave Solomon special instructions regarding Shimei, of whose fidelity he seems to have been in doubt (1 Kings 2:8,9). He was put to death at the command of Solomon, because he had violated his word by leaving Jerusalem and going to Gath to recover two of his servants who had escaped (36-46). (3.) One of David’s mighty men who refused to acknowledge Adonijah as David’s successor (1 Kings 1:8). He is probably the same person who is called elsewhere (4:18) “the son of Elah.” (4.) A son of Pedaiah, the brother of Zerubbabel (1 Chronicles 3:19). (5.) A Simeonite (1 Chronicles 4:26, 27). (6.) A Reubenite (1 Chronicles 5:4). (7.) A Levite of the family of Gershon (1 Chronicles 6:42). (8.) A Ramathite who was “over the vineyards” of David (1 Chronicles 27:27). (9.) One of the sons of Heman, who assisted in the purification of the temple (2 Chronicles 29:14). (10.) A Levite (2 Chronicles 31:12, 13). (11.) Another Levite (Ezra 10:23). “The family of Shimei” (Zechariah 12:13; R.V., “the family of the Shimeites”) were the descendants of Shimei (1).

↩ ◇ Note. The Levite-firstborn substitution. Yahweh instructs Moses to count the firstborn males of all Israel and the Levites separately, then substitute the Levites for the firstborn (3:45). The theological logic: every firstborn male in Israel is technically Yahweh’s (Exod 13:2, the Passover-night theology), but rather than physical service from each firstborn, Yahweh accepts the Levitical tribe as collective substitute. Where Levite numbers fell short of the firstborn count, the surplus firstborn were redeemed at five shekels each (3:46–51). The arrangement is one of the OT’s clearest cases of substitutionary cultic logic — one group serving in place of another by divine appointment — and it underwrites the entire later theology of the priesthood as set apart for sanctuary work that the rest of Israel could not perform. The principle of substitution becomes important in Christian theological reflection on Christ’s priestly office (Heb 7–10), explicitly drawing on this OT pattern.

↩ ◇ Note. The Kohathite carrying duty. The Kohathites — descendants of Levi’s second son — bear the most sacred objects (ark, table, lampstand, altars), but the chapter is explicit that they may not see or touch the holy things directly: Aaron and his sons must first cover everything with the prescribed coverings, and only then may the Kohathites lift the wrapped objects by their poles. Touching the uncovered objects results in death (4:15, 18–20; cf. the death of Uzzah in 2 Sam 6:6–7, who breaks this exact rule). The provision establishes a graded-access principle that runs through Israelite cult: the sacred is never simply forbidden but accessible according to specific procedure, and procedural violation has consequences regardless of intent. The Christian appropriation of the Kohathite imagery in Heb 9:1–14 takes the elaborate covering procedure as type — multiple veils between the worshipper and the holy — that the high-priestly entry of Christ supersedes.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: LEVITES.

↩ ◇ Note. The Levitical service age. The chapter sets Levitical sanctuary service from age 25 to 50 (8:24–25), with elders 50+ continuing in lighter advisory roles ("they shall keep the watch" but no longer carry burdens). The age-range differs slightly from Num 4:3 (which begins at 30) — most rabbinic and modern readers (so Milgrom) reconcile this by treating 25–30 as preparatory training and 30–50 as full service. The institution of mandatory retirement at 50 is highly unusual in ANE priesthood traditions, where lifelong service was standard; the Levitical retirement registers an Israelite-specific recognition that the physical demands of sanctuary work (especially carrying the tabernacle structures during the wilderness period) exceeded the strength of older men. The principle of role-shift with age — from active service to advisory eldership — becomes structural in later Israelite institutional life.

↩ ◇ Note. Departure from Sinai. The verse marks one of the structural pivots of the Pentateuch: the cloud of Yahweh’s presence lifts from the tabernacle, and Israel begins moving toward the promised land for the first time. The encampment at Sinai has lasted approximately eleven months (cf. Exod 19:1, when they arrived; the date here is the second month of the second year — about eleven months later). Sinai itself was always meant as way-station; what looks in narrative terms like the major plot-event of Exodus–Numbers (the giving of the law) is, in geographic terms, a long pause in a journey that resumes here. The cloud’s movement is itself the OT’s clearest articulation of the divine-direction-by-meteorological-sign principle: Israel does not march by Moses’ schedule but by the cloud’s lifting (cf. 9:15–23). The passage establishes the pattern by which Israel will navigate the rest of the wilderness period — divine guidance manifest as visible meteorological phenomenon.

↩ ◇ Note. Caleb’s minority report. Twelve spies are sent into Canaan; ten return with a defeatist report ("we are not able… they are stronger than we are," 13:31), and two — Caleb (here) and Joshua (14:6–9) — argue for immediate invasion. The narrative carefully distinguishes the two minority reports from each other: Caleb’s here is purely military-pragmatic ("we are well able to overcome it"); Joshua’s in 14:9 is theological ("Yahweh is with us, do not fear them"). Together they represent the dual ground of OT confidence — practical capability combined with covenant trust. The episode becomes the great paradigm-event of unbelief in OT theology: Israel’s rejection of Caleb and Joshua’s counsel produces forty years of wilderness wandering, and the entire generation dies in the wilderness as a result. The Letter to the Hebrews (3:7–4:11) takes this episode as the foundational warning narrative for Christian perseverance — failure at the critical decision point becomes the model of all failure to enter "rest."

↩ ◇ Note. The priestly portion. The chapter codifies the priesthood’s economic support: every devoted thing (ḥerem) in Israel becomes priestly property, including firstfruits, firstborn animal redemption fees, tithes, and various offerings. The arrangement substitutes for a tribal land-portion (cf. 18:20, "you shall have no inheritance in their land"): Levites and priests are economically dependent on the offerings of the rest of Israel for their entire livelihood. The system is brilliant institutionally — it prevents priestly land-accumulation, embeds priestly welfare in covenant compliance by all Israel, and creates a permanent economic incentive for the priesthood to preserve the offering system — but it is also fragile. When tithing breaks down (cf. Neh 13:10, Mal 3:8–10), the priesthood collapses immediately. The verse and the surrounding chapter encode one of the OT’s most consequential institutional designs, with effects running through the entire history of Israelite religion.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Numbers (c. 365 AD)

On the red heifer 'wherein is no blemish, and upon which never came yoke' (Num 19:2), Ephrem reads the unyoked, unblemished, wholly-burnt red heifer as the canonical Old-Testament type of Christ's atoning sacrifice — taken up explicitly by Hebrews 9:13-14 as the lesser-to-greater argument: if the ashes of a heifer sanctified the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ purge the conscience. The red colour anticipates the blood, the unyoked freedom anticipates Christ's voluntary submission, the outside-the-camp burning anticipates Calvary outside Jerusalem (Heb 13:11-12). Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Num 19 + Heb 9 as canonical doubled-witness to Christ's once-for-all purifying sacrifice.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). YOKE (1.) Fitted on the neck of oxen for the purpose of binding to them the traces by which they might draw the plough, etc. (Numbers 19:2; Deuteronomy 21:3). It was a curved piece of wood called ’ol. (2.) In Jeremiah 27:2; 28:10, 12 the word in the Authorized Version rendered “yoke” is motah, which properly means a “staff,” or as in the Revised Version, “bar.” These words in the Hebrew are both used figuratively of severe bondage, or affliction, or subjection (Leviticus 26:13; 1 Kings 12:4; Isaiah 47:6; Lamentations 1:14; 3:27). In the New Testament the word “yoke” is also used to denote servitude (Matthew 11:29, 30; Acts 15:10; Galatians 5:1). (3.) In 1 Samuel 11:7, 1 Kings 19:21, Job 1:3 the word thus translated is tzemed, which signifies a pair, two oxen yoked or coupled together, and hence in 1 Samuel 14:14 it represents as much land as a yoke of oxen could plough in a day, like the Latin jugum. In Isaiah 5:10 this word in the plural is translated “acres.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ASHES The ashes of a red heifer burned entire (Numbers 19:5) when sprinkled on the unclean made them ceremonially clean (Hebrews 9:13). To cover the head with ashes was a token of self-abhorrence and humiliation (2 Samuel 13:19; Esther 4:3; Jeremiah 6:26, etc.). To feed on ashes (Isaiah 44:20), means to seek that which will prove to be vain and unsatisfactory, and hence it denotes the unsatisfactory nature of idol-worship. (Comp. Hos. 12:1).

↩ ◇ Note. The red heifer ashes. The chapter describes one of the OT’s strangest rituals: a perfectly red heifer is slaughtered outside the camp, burned in its entirety (with cedar, hyssop, and scarlet thread added), and the ashes preserved as the active ingredient of "water of impurity" used to purify those who have touched a corpse. The ritual is unique in three ways: (1) it produces the only purification-substance the OT prescribes for corpse-contamination; (2) it is performed outside the sanctuary, not inside; (3) it has the paradoxical property of purifying those it cleanses while defiling those who handle it. The red heifer is the great rabbinic puzzle (Num. R. 19:1; the ritual is treated as a chuq — a divine decree whose reasoning is hidden). The Letter to the Hebrews (9:13–14) takes the ashes-of-the-heifer ritual as the definitive OT type for the cleansing power of Christ’s blood, drawing on the paradox that the death of the offering produces life for the recipients. Few OT rituals have so theologically charged a Christian afterlife.

↩ ◇ Note. The third Balaam oracle. Balaam’s involuntary blessing of Israel’s encamped tents is one of the OT’s most influential single verses in Jewish liturgy: the phrase Mah tovu ohalekha Ya‘akov ("How goodly are your tents, O Jacob") becomes the opening line of the daily Jewish morning prayer, recited on entering the synagogue. The verse functions theologically as the inversion-blessing par excellence: a hired prophet, brought by an enemy king specifically to curse Israel, is overcome by Yahweh’s spirit and speaks blessing instead — exactly the curse-into-blessing reversal that runs through the patriarchal narratives (Gen 12:3, where Abraham is promised that those who curse him will themselves be cursed). The chapter is one of the OT’s clearest portraits of Yahweh’s control over speech and prophecy: even the words of a non-Israelite professional curse-pronouncer become channels for divine blessing. The same Balaam will be condemned later (Num 31:8, 16; 2 Pet 2:15; Rev 2:14) for his subsequent counsel that brought the Baal-Peor catastrophe — the chapter holds his moment of inspired oracle in tension with his later moral failure.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ABEL-SHITTIM meadow of the acacias, frequently called simply “Shittim” (Numbers 25:1; Joshua 2:1; Micah 6:5), a place on the east of Jordan, in the plain of Moab, nearly opposite Jericho. It was the forty-second encampment of the Israelites, their last resting-place before they crossed the Jordan (Numbers 33:49; 22:1; 26:3; 31:12; comp. 25:1; 31:16).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ZIMRI praise-worthy. (1.) A son of Salu, slain by Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, because of his wickedness in bringing a Midianitish woman into his tent (Numbers 25:6-15). (2.) Murdered Elah at Tirzah, and succeeded him on the throne of Israel (1 Kings 16:8-10). He reigned only seven days, for Omri, whom the army elected as king, laid siege to Tirzah, whereupon Zimri set fire to the palace and perished amid its ruins (11-20). Omri succeeded to the throne only after four years of fierce war with Tibni, another claimant to the throne.

↩ ◇ Note. Phinehas’s zeal. Phinehas — Aaron’s grandson — runs an Israelite man and a Midianite woman through with a single spear-thrust during the Baal-Peor apostasy. The text presents the act not as judicial murder but as zealous intervention: 25:11 specifically commends Phinehas for "turning away" Yahweh’s wrath from Israel, and 25:13 grants him "a covenant of perpetual priesthood" — establishing the Phinehas line as the high-priestly succession until Eli’s deposition (1 Sam 2:30) and Zadok’s reinstatement (1 Kgs 2:35; cf. 1 Chr 6:4–8 for the genealogy). The episode becomes the OT’s paradigm-text for "zeal" (qin’ah) — religious-political action outside normal judicial procedure to defend covenant integrity. The Maccabees explicitly cite Phinehas as their model (1 Macc 2:26, 54), and the Zealot movement of the first century CE took its name from this same biblical model. The verse is theologically and ethically charged: it has been read both as endorsement of righteous violent intervention and as deeply troubling for any modern reader. Few OT episodes have so contested a moral legacy.

↩ ◇ Note. The festival calendar. Numbers 28–29 sets out the most complete calendar of Israelite cultic offerings in the Pentateuch — daily, weekly (Sabbath), monthly (new moon), and annual (Passover, Shavuot, the seventh-month sequence of New Year, Day of Atonement, and Sukkot). The catalog organizes Israelite time around layered cycles of offering, with each level intensifying as the temporal unit increases. The Sabbath offering specifically — two extra lambs beyond the daily two (28:3) — is one of the OT’s clearest demonstrations that Sabbath rest does not mean cultic rest: more sacrifice is required on the Sabbath than on weekdays. The two-tier framing of the Sabbath (rest for Israel, intensified worship in the sanctuary) becomes one of the structural features of Jewish liturgical life. Jesus’ argument about the priests in the temple "profaning the Sabbath" (Matt 12:5) by working on it draws directly on this verse — the Sabbath sanctuary work is the OT-given exception that proves the rule.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BALAAM Lord of the people; foreigner or glutton, as interpreted by others, the son of Beor, was a man of some rank among the Midianites (Numbers 31:8; comp. 16). He resided at Pethor (Deuteronomy 23:4), in Mesopotamia (Numbers 23:7). It is evident that though dwelling among idolaters he had some knowledge of the true God; and was held in such reputation that it was supposed that he whom he blessed was blessed, and he whom he cursed was cursed. When the Israelites were encamped on the plains of Moab, on the east of Jordan, by Jericho, Balak sent for Balaam “from Aram, out of the mountains of the east,” to curse them; but by the remarkable interposition of God he was utterly unable to fulfil Balak’s wish, however desirous he was to do so. The apostle Peter refers (2 Peter 2:15, 16) to this as an historical event. In Micah 6:5 reference also is made to the relations between Balaam and Balak. Though Balaam could not curse Israel, yet he suggested a mode by which the divine displeasure might be caused to descend upon them (Numbers 25). In a battle between Israel and the Midianites (q.v.) Balaam was slain while fighting on the side of Balak (Numbers 31:8). The “doctrine of Balaam” is spoken of in Revelation 2:14, in allusion to the fact that it was through the teaching of Balaam that Balak learned the way by which the Israelites might be led into sin. (See NICOLAITANES.) Balaam was constrained to utter prophecies regarding the future of Israel of wonderful magnificence and beauty of expression (Numbers 24:5-9, 17).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). REBA fourth, one of the Midianite chiefs slain by the Israelites in the wilderness (Numbers 31:8; Joshua 13:21).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). REKEM embroidered; variegated. (1.) One of the five Midianite kings whom the Israelites destroyed (Numbers 31:8). (2.) One of the sons of Hebron (1 Chronicles 2:43, 44). (3.) A town of Benjamin (Joshua 18:27).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ZUR rock. (1.) One of the five Midianite kings whom the Israelites defeated and put to death (Numbers 31:8). (2.) A Benjamite (1 Chronicles 8:30).

↩ ◇ Note. The Midianite war. The chapter is one of the most ethically difficult passages in the entire Pentateuch — Moses orders the slaughter of all Midianite male children and all non-virgin Midianite women, with virgin girls distributed among the Israelite warriors. Modern readers find the passage agonizing; ancient and medieval Jewish and Christian commentators struggled with it as well. Several interpretive moves attempt to make sense of it: contextual (Midianite women had been the agents of the Baal-Peor seduction in ch 25, so the targeting is specific to that crisis), source-critical (the chapter reflects post-exilic ideological idealizing rather than historical practice), or ethical-progressivist (the OT honestly portrays warfare as the ancient world conducted it, and the canon contains material whose moral weight Israel itself eventually disowned, cf. the prophetic critiques of ḥerem theology). No reading entirely defuses the difficulty; the chapter is one of the OT texts where serious engagement requires acknowledging that biblical material includes commands that the canon’s own later voices (and later interpretive communities) have not been able to receive without grief.

↩ ◇ Note. The lot principle, again. The chapter restates the principle established in Num 26: tribal allotments will be assigned by lot. The doubled emphasis (here and in 26:55–56, then operationalized in Josh 14–19) registers the theological seriousness of randomized divine assignment — no tribe can claim it earned its specific territory through political maneuvering or military prowess, because the location was given by lot before the conquest began. The provision has had long influence: Catholic and Reformed traditions alike have appealed to OT lot-casting as a legitimate decision-procedure when divine guidance is sought without clear scriptural direction (Acts 1:26, the apostolic selection of Matthias; the Moravian Brethren’s historical use of lot for major communal decisions). The verse closes Numbers’ extended treatment of land-allotment theology and prepares for its actual implementation in Joshua. The chapter ends not with the conquest itself — Numbers stops short of that — but with the principles by which the conquest will be administered.

Another of David’s sons (1 Chronicles 3:6). (4.) A priest sent by Jehoshaphat to teach the people the law (2 Chronicles 17:8).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GAMALIEL reward of God. (1.) A chief of the tribe of Manasseh at the census at Sinai (Numbers 1:10; 2:20; 7:54, 59). (2.) The son of rabbi Simeon, and grandson of the famous rabbi Hillel. He was a Pharisse, and therefore the opponent of the party of the Sadducees. He was noted for his learning, and was president of the Sanhedrim during the regins of Tiberius, Caligula, and Claudius, and died, it is said, about eighteen years before the destruction of Jerusalem. When the apostles were brought before the council, charged with preaching the resurrection of Jesus, as a zealous Pharisee Gamaliel councelled moderation and calmness. By a reference to well-known events, he advised them to “refrain from these men.” If their work or counsel was of man, it would come to nothing; but if it was of God, they could not destroy it, and therefore ought to be on their guard lest they should be “found fighting against God” (Acts 5:34-40). Paul was one of his disciples (22:3).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PEDAHZUR rock of redemption, the father of Gamaliel and prince of Manasseh at the time of the Exodus (Numbers 1:10; 2:20).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). REUBEN , TRIBE OF at the Exodus numbered 46,500 male adults, from twenty years old and upwards (Numbers 1:20, 21), and at the close of the wilderness wanderings they numbered only 43,730 (26:7). This tribe united with that of Gad in asking permission to settle in the “land of Gilead,” “on the other side of Jordan” (32:1-5). The lot assigned to Reuben was the smallest of the lots given to the trans-Jordanic tribes. It extended from the Arnon, in the south along the coast of the Dead Sea to its northern end, where the Jordan flows into it (Joshua 13:15-21, 23). It thus embraced the original kingdom of Sihon. Reuben is “to the eastern tribes what Simeon is to the western. ‘Unstable as water,’ he vanishes away into a mere Arabian tribe. ‘His men are few;’ it is all he can do ‘to live and not die.’ We hear of nothing beyond the multiplication of their cattle in the land of Gilead, their spoils of ‘camels fifty thousand, and of asses two thousand’ (1 Chronicles 5:9, 10, 20, 21). In the great struggles of the nation he never took part. The complaint against him in the song of Deborah is the summary of his whole history. ‘By the streams of Reuben,’ i.e., by the fresh streams which descend from the eastern hills into the Jordan and the Dead Sea, on whose banks the Bedouin chiefs met then as now to debate, in the ‘streams’ of Reuben great were the ‘desires’”, i.e., resolutions which were never carried out, the people idly resting among their flocks as if it were a time of peace (Judges 5:15, 16). Stanley’s Sinai and Palestine. All the three tribes on the east of Jordan at length fell into complete apostasy, and the time of retribution came. God “stirred up the spirit of Pul, king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria,” to carry them away, the first of the tribes, into captivity (1 Chronicles 5:25, 26).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ZEBULUN , TRIBE OF numbered at Sinai (Numbers 1:31) and before entering Canaan (26:27). It was one of the tribes which did not drive out the Canaanites, but only made them tributary (Judges 1:30). It took little interest in public affairs. It responded, however, readily to the summons of Gideon (6:35), and afterwards assisted in enthroning David at Hebron (1 Chronicles 12:33, 40). Along with the other northern tribes, Zebulun was carried away into the land of Assyria by Tiglath-pileser (2 Kings 15:29). In Deborah’s song the words, “Out of Zebulun they that handle the pen of the writer” (Judges 5:14) has been rendered in the R.V., “They that handle the marshal’s staff.” This is a questionable rendering. “The word sopher (‘scribe’ or ‘writer’) defines the word shebhet (‘rod’ or ‘pen’) with which it is conjoined. The ‘rod of the scribe’ on the Assyrian monuments was the stylus of wood or metal, with the help of which the clay tablet was engraved, or the papyrus inscribed with characters. The scribe who wielded it was the associate and assistant of the ‘lawgivers.’” (Sayce).

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Numbers (c. 365 AD)

On the setting-apart of the Levites for tabernacle service, Ephrem reads the census-and-separation pattern of Num 1:50 as the canonical model for ordered ministry: the people are numbered for their tribes, but one tribe is numbered for the Lord himself. The Levites' exemption from the military census is not privilege but conscription into a more dangerous service — the daily handling of the holy things. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Num 1:50 as the Old-Testament warrant for the consecration of the däbtära and the priest-monks; the consecrated are numbered for the sanctuary first, for the nation only afterward.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BANNER (1.) The flag or banner of the larger kind, serving for three tribes marching together. These standards, of which there were four, were worked with embroidery and beautifully ornamented (Numbers 1:52; 2:2, 3, 10, 18, 25; Cant. 2:4; 6:4, 10). (2.) The flag borne by each separate tribe, of a smaller form. Probably it bore on it the name of the tribe to which it belonged, or some distinguishing device (Numbers 2:2,34). (3.) A lofty signal-flag, not carried about, but stationary. It was usually erected on a mountain or other lofty place. As soon as it was seen the war-trumpets were blown (Psalm 60:4; Isaiah 5:26; 11:12; 13:2; 18:3; 30:17; Jeremiah 4:6 21; Ezekiel 27:7). (4.) A “sign of fire” (Jeremiah 6:1) was sometimes used as a signal. The banners and ensigns of the Roman army had idolatrous images upon them, and hence they are called the “abomination of desolation” (q.v.). The principal Roman standard, however, was an eagle. (See Matthew 24:28; Luke 17:37, where the Jewish nation is compared to a dead body, which the eagles gather together to devour.) God’s setting up or giving a banner (Psalm 20:5; 60:4; Cant. 2:4) imports his presence and protection and aid extended to his people.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Numbers (c. 365 AD)

On the cloud covering the tabernacle by day and the appearance-of-fire by night (Num 9:15), Ephrem reads the doubled pillar — cloud and fire — as the canonical visible-sign of continuous divine indwelling: the Lord neither withdraws by day nor leaves the camp dark by night. The same cloud that veiled Sinai's fire now veils and reveals the tabernacle's glory. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Num 9:15 as the canonical anchor of the perpetual veil-and-glory pattern preserved in the curtained sanctuary: the tabot is veiled in cloud, illumined by lampstand fire, both signs of the abiding Lord.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). JOURNEY (1.) A day’s journey in the East is from 16 to 20 miles (Numbers 11:31). (2.) A Sabbath-day’s journey is 2,000 paces or yards from the city walls (Acts 1:12). According to Jewish tradition, it was the distance one might travel without violating the law of Exodus 16:29. (See SABBATH.)
